# Central Africa Regiment

The Central Africa Regiment was a British colonial military unit that served in what is now Malawi during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It was formed in 1896 as the British Central African Rifles and underwent two name changes before being amalgamated into the King's African Rifles in 1902 . The regiment was notable for its service in several campaigns across Africa, including the suppression of the Ngoni Rebellion, the War of the Golden Stool, and operations against the "Mad Mullah" in Somaliland .

## 1. History

### 1.1 Formation and Early Years

The Central Africa Regiment traces its origins to 1896 when it was established as the British Central African Rifles . The force was initially composed of 738 African troops and 175 Sikh soldiers . This multi-ethnic composition reflected the British colonial strategy of maintaining a mixed force with both local African recruits and Indian troops serving as a stabilizing element.

In 1898, the unit underwent its first name change, dropping the word "British" from its title to become simply the Central African Rifles . This renaming was significant as it marked a shift in the British colonial administration's approach to local military forces, signaling a move toward greater Africanization of the unit's identity while maintaining British command structure.

The following year, in 1899, the force was renamed once more to become the Central Africa Regiment . This final name change occurred shortly before the regiment was to participate in several major military campaigns that would define its legacy.

### 1.2 Campaigns and Operations

The Central Africa Regiment saw extensive action in several military campaigns across Africa. In 1898, the regiment, along with its Indian contingent, played a crucial role in suppressing the Ngoni Rebellion in northeastern Rhodesia . During this campaign, the regiment's seven-pounder guns were used "with great effect" against the rebels .

One of the regiment's most significant victories came on September 30, 1899, when it fought in the Battle of Obassa, achieving a decisive victory that led to the end of a war . The exact nature of this conflict and its broader context remain somewhat unclear from available sources, but the battle is noted as a key moment in the regiment's history.

In 1900, elements of the Central Africa Regiment were deployed to the Gold Coast (modern-day Ghana) to participate in the War of the Golden Stool against the Asante Empire . This conflict, also known as the Yaa Asantewaa War, was a major uprising against British colonial rule . Half of the regiment's battalion was sent to the Gold Coast, while the other half was engaged in suppressing an uprising in the Gambia Colony and Protectorate .

The regiment also participated in the Somaliland campaign against Muhammad ibn 'Abdallah Hassan, known to the British as the "Mad Mullah" . This campaign, which lasted from 1900 to 1920, was a series of conflicts between the British and the Dervishes led by Hassan . The Central Africa Regiment's involvement in these operations helped earn it a reputation "rare amongst colonial troops for their skills and professionalism" .

### 1.3 Amalgamation into the King's African Rifles

On January 1, 1902, the Central Africa Regiment was amalgamated with the East Africa Rifles and Uganda Rifles to form the King's African Rifles (KAR) . This reorganization was part of a broader effort to centralize British colonial military forces in East Africa and create a more unified command structure .

The formation of the KAR created six battalions, with the Central Africa Regiment contributing the 1st (Nyasaland) Battalion and the 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalion . These battalions were also known as the 1st and 2nd Central African Battalions . At the time of formation, the King's African Rifles included 4,683 men, including 104 British officers .

## 2. Organization and Structure

### 2.1 Initial Composition

The Central Africa Regiment initially consisted of six companies with distinct ethnic compositions . Company A, D, and E were nominally Tonga, Companies B and C were Yao, and Company F was composed of Chewa and Ngoni . This ethnic organization reflected the British colonial strategy of maintaining separate units based on tribal affiliations, which was believed to reduce the risk of unified resistance while leveraging traditional leadership structures.

### 2.2 Command Structure

The Central Africa Regiment was commanded by several notable British officers. Alfred Sharpe and Willoughby Verner are specifically mentioned as notable commanders . These officers were responsible for leading the regiment through its various campaigns and maintaining discipline among the diverse ethnic groups within the unit.

The command structure followed the typical British colonial model, with British officers in command positions and non-commissioned officers (NCOs) drawn from both British and Indian ranks. This structure provided a chain of command that was familiar to British military doctrine while allowing for some cultural adaptation in dealing with African troops.

### 2.3 Size and Strength

The Central Africa Regiment varied in size during its existence, typically maintaining between one and two battalions . The exact strength of the regiment at any given time is not precisely documented, but historical records indicate that it was comparable in size to other colonial units of the period.

When the regiment was amalgamated into the King's African Rifles in 1902, its contribution included two full battalions. The 1st (Nyasaland) Battalion served from 1902 to 1964, while the 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalion served from 1902 to 1963 . These battalions were later incorporated into the independent nations' armies, with the 1st Battalion becoming the 1st Battalion, Malawi Rifles, and the 2nd Battalion becoming the 2nd Battalion, Northern Rhodesia Regiment (later Zambia Regiment) .

## 3. Equipment and Uniforms

### 3.1 Weaponry

The Central Africa Regiment was equipped with standard British colonial military weapons of the period. Historical records indicate that the regiment had access to seven-pounder guns, which were used effectively during the suppression of the Ngoni Rebellion in 1898 . These weapons were particularly valuable in African campaigns where they could breach mud walls and wooden stockades and break up concentrations of warriors .

The infantrymen were likely equipped with the standard British service rifles of the time, which would have included the Martini-Henry rifle and later the Lee-Metford or Lee-Enfield rifles. The regiment's Indian contingent would have been armed similarly to British Indian Army units of the period.

### 3.2 Uniforms and Insignia

While specific details about the Central Africa Regiment's uniforms are limited, it can be inferred from historical context that they followed the general pattern of British colonial forces in Africa. The regiment's successor units in the King's African Rifles wore distinctive uniforms that included blue jerseys with khaki shorts and blue puttees, along with red fezzes (tarboosh) .

The 1st and 2nd Battalions of the Central Africa Regiment (later part of KAR) were noted for wearing black fezzes rather than the standard red ones . This distinctive headgear may have been unique to the Central African units and served as a way to distinguish them from other battalions in the King's African Rifles.

## 4. Legacy and Impact

### 4.1 Transformation into National Armies

The Central Africa Regiment's legacy extends beyond its six-year existence as an independent unit. When the various territories from which it was recruited gained independence, the regiment's successor units were incorporated into the new national armies . The 1st Battalion became the 1st Battalion, Malawi Rifles, while the 2nd Battalion became the 2nd Battalion, Northern Rhodesia Regiment, which later became part of the Zambia Regiment .

This transformation represented the culmination of a process that began with the regiment's formation in 1896. The British colonial military structure, with its emphasis on discipline, organization, and modern weaponry, provided a foundation for the armed forces of the newly independent nations of Malawi and Zambia.

### 4.2 Military Traditions and Customs

The Central Africa Regiment established several military traditions that were carried forward by its successor units. The use of English as the common language of command, for example, was maintained even when former members of the regiment served in German forces . When German forces in East Africa recruited former 2nd Central Africa Battalion soldiers in 1911, they retained English as the language of command and even kept British bugle calls .

The regiment's reputation for professionalism and skill in combat also influenced later military forces. The Central Africa Regiment earned a reputation "rare amongst colonial troops for their skills and professionalism" through its service in various campaigns . This reputation helped establish a standard of military excellence that was maintained by the Malawi Rifles and other successor units.

### 4.3 Historical Significance

The Central Africa Regiment holds an important place in the military history of British colonial Africa. It was one of the three original regiments (along with the East Africa Rifles and Uganda Rifles) that formed the foundation of the King's African Rifles in 1902 . The KAR went on to become one of the most famous colonial military units, serving with distinction in both World Wars and various colonial campaigns.

The regiment's formation in 1896 marked a significant development in British colonial military policy in Africa. It represented a shift from ad hoc local levies to more professional, organized military units that could be deployed across different territories as needed. The regiment's participation in campaigns across Africa, from the Gold Coast to Somaliland, demonstrated the flexibility and effectiveness of this approach.

The Central Africa Regiment also played a role in the broader context of British imperial expansion and consolidation in Africa. Its campaigns helped establish and maintain British control over territories that would later become part of modern Malawi, Zambia, and other African nations. The regiment's legacy thus extends beyond military history into the broader story of African colonialism and independence.

## 5. Commanders and Notable Personnel

### 5.1 Commanding Officers

The Central Africa Regiment was led by several notable British officers during its six-year existence. Alfred Sharpe and Willoughby Verner are specifically identified as notable commanders of the regiment . These officers were selected for their experience in African colonial warfare and their ability to command multi-ethnic forces effectively.

Colonel William Manning, while not specifically identified as a commander of the Central Africa Regiment, had significant connections to the unit. Manning commanded operations against Chief Mpezeni in northeast Rhodesia in 1898, for which he was promoted to brevet major in 1898 and brevet lieutenant-colonel in 1899 ). During the Anglo-Boer War, Manning was noted as a spectator at a military event where a "dusky and handsome fellow of the 1st battalion central africa regiment" was in attendance .

### 5.2 Other Notable Personnel

Alexander Cobbe served as second-in-command of the 1st Battalion, Central African Rifles, in October 1899, with the local rank of captain . Cobbe's appointment highlights the British military's practice of appointing experienced officers to command colonial units, even at the battalion level.

The regiment also included Indian soldiers from the 23rd and 32nd Pioneers and Hyderabad Lancers, who served as a nucleus for the police force in Central Africa . These Indian troops provided valuable experience and stability to the predominantly African regiment, serving as both trainers and reliable fighting men until the loyalty and effectiveness of the local troops could be ensured.

## 6. Operations and Campaigns

### 6.1 The Ngoni Rebellion (1898)

One of the Central Africa Regiment's earliest major campaigns was the suppression of the Ngoni Rebellion in 1898 in northeastern Rhodesia (modern-day Zambia) . The regiment's Indian contingent, along with their seven-pounder guns, played a crucial role in this campaign. The guns were particularly effective against the Ngoni warriors, who fought from mud-walled villages and stockades .

The Ngoni were a powerful warrior people who had migrated from southern Africa and established themselves in what is now Malawi and Zambia. Their rebellion threatened British colonial authority in the region, and the Central Africa Regiment's successful suppression of this uprising helped establish British control over the area.

### 6.2 The War of the Golden Stool (1900)

In 1900, the Central Africa Regiment was called upon to participate in the War of the Golden Stool, also known as the Yaa Asantewaa War or the Third Ashanti Expedition . This conflict arose when the British attempted to find the sacred Golden Stool of the Ashanti people, which was considered the throne of the Ashanti Empire and the symbol of their nationhood.

Half of the Central Africa Regiment's battalion was deployed to the Gold Coast (modern-day Ghana) to participate in this campaign, while the other half was engaged in suppressing an uprising in the Gambia Colony and Protectorate . This simultaneous deployment across different territories demonstrated the regiment's versatility and the British colonial authorities' confidence in its capabilities.

Historical records mention a Captain who served as a special service officer attached to the 2nd Battalion Central Africa Regiment during the Ashanti 1900 campaign. This officer was one of two British officers who participated in the capture of the powerful Ashanti chief Kobina Cherri at Su in Jam .

### 6.3 The Somaliland Campaign

The Central Africa Regiment also participated in the Somaliland campaign against Muhammad ibn 'Abdallah Hassan, known to the British as the "Mad Mullah" . This campaign was part of a series of conflicts between the British and the Dervishes that lasted from 1900 to 1920 .

Hassan led a holy war against British, Italian, and Ethiopian colonial intrusions in the Somali peninsula . The Central Africa Regiment's involvement in these operations was part of a broader British effort to maintain control over their Somaliland protectorate. The regiment's service in these difficult campaigns, fighting in harsh desert conditions against determined opponents, helped establish its reputation for professionalism and skill.

### 6.4 The Battle of Obassa

The Battle of Obassa, which took place on September 30, 1899, was a decisive victory for the Central Africa Regiment . The battle resulted in the end of a war, though the specific conflict and its broader context are not clearly documented in the available sources.

This victory was significant enough to be specifically mentioned in historical records as a key moment in the regiment's history. The decisive nature of the victory suggests that it was a major engagement that had far-reaching consequences for British colonial control in the region where it occurred.

## 7. Conclusion

The Central Africa Regiment, though it existed for only six years (1896-1902), played a significant role in the military history of British colonial Africa. From its formation as the British Central African Rifles to its amalgamation into the King's African Rifles, the regiment served as a crucial instrument of British imperial policy in Central and East Africa.

The regiment's military campaigns demonstrated its versatility and effectiveness across different African territories and against various opponents. Whether fighting the Ngoni in Rhodesia, participating in the War of the Golden Stool in the Gold Coast, or campaigning against the Mad Mullah in Somaliland, the Central Africa Regiment consistently performed with the professionalism that earned it a reputation "rare amongst colonial troops" .

The legacy of the Central Africa Regiment extends beyond its immediate military contributions. Through its successor units in the King's African Rifles and eventually in the national armies of Malawi and Zambia, the regiment helped establish military traditions and organizational structures that continue to influence African military forces today. The regiment's use of English as the common language of command, its emphasis on discipline and training, and its integration of different ethnic groups within a unified military structure all became lasting features of African military organizations.

The Central Africa Regiment thus stands as an important example of how colonial military forces shaped the development of modern African nations. While its primary purpose was to serve British imperial interests, the regiment also contributed to the modernization of military forces in the territories where it served, providing a foundation for the professional armies of independent Africa.

The regiment's history also highlights broader themes in the study of colonial military forces, including the challenges of commanding multi-ethnic troops, the adaptation of European military methods to African conditions, and the complex relationships between colonial powers and indigenous populations. Through its six years of service, the Central Africa Regiment left an indelible mark on the military and political history of Central Africa, a legacy that continues to resonate in the nations that emerged from the British colonial empire.

**East Africa**. Also includes **other parts of Africa**, including **West Africa**, but see the separate page for **[South Africa](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/South_Africa "South Africa")**.

Also see
--------

*   [General Register Office](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/General_Register_Office "General Register Office") [United Kingdom] for general information about birth, marriage and death records for British nationals abroad.
*   [Society of Genealogists](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Society_of_Genealogists "Society of Genealogists"), London for details of some records from Africa, including inscriptions from Basutoland, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Nyasaland, Sierra Leone and Uganda.

During WW1, some German civilians were transferred from East Africa to camps at [Ahmednagar](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Ahmadnagar "Ahmadnagar") and [Belgaum](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Belgaum "Belgaum") in India.
*   [Second World War](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Second_World_War "Second World War")

Information about the database African Newspapers, Series 1 and 2, 1800-1925; and African Newspapers: The British Library Collection, both part of Readex World Newspapers Archive, both of which are available at the British Library. Also information about a database containing a collection of African _Blue Books_ from thirteen colonies across Africa, also available at the British Library.
British African regiments such as the King's African Rifles
-----------------------------------------------------------

Excludes [South Africa](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/South_Africa "South Africa").

After Uganda was declared a Protectorate in 1893, the colonial authorities formed a military force of some 600 regulars and 300 reservists, most of whom were Sudanese recruited in Egypt. A small number of Arabic-speaking British officers were responsible for training this force. In 1895 this force was organized into rifle companies, which collectively became known as the "Uganda Rifles".

Growing disillusionment in the Uganda Rifles over issues such as loneliness, poor food, poor pay and frequent reassignments to remote areas led to a mutiny in 1897. Several British officers were killed, and discontent amongst Uganda’s moslem community, which was sympathetic to the Sudanese, erupted into violence in several places. The British despatched troops from India to put down the mutiny and to stop the violence, although this took until 1899 to complete.

As a result of the mutiny, towards the end of 1897 the colonial government decided to reorganise the Uganda Rifles on an urgent basis, and a number of commissioned and non-commissioned officers for the task of reorganisation were recruited in London. A newspaper report of the day said ,,,The Soudanese forming the force will be greatly reduced, and the vacancies filled up by recruiting from the East African Protectorate and, possibly, also from India… The non-commissioned officers were ready to depart for Uganda around 20th-21st January 1898, and the commissioned officers followed in due course.[[1]](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/East_Africa#cite_note-1)

The King's African Rifles (KAR) was formed on 1 January 1902 from various local regiments, and were responsible for the defence of British colonies and protectorates in East Africa, initially Nyasaland, Kenya, Uganda, British Somaliland, and later Tanganyika Territory and Zanzibar. Each colony was responsible for recruiting and maintaining its own battalions.[[2]](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/East_Africa#cite_note-2) The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions [later Regiments] were established from the Central African Regiment, 3rd (Kenya) Battalion [later Regiment] from the East Africa Rifles, 4th and 5th (Uganda) Battalions [later Regiments] from the Uganda Rifles, and 6th (Somaliland) Battalion [later Regiment] from local Somaliland forces. In 1910 this was disbanded, though a 6th (Tanganyika) Regiment emerged in 1917.[[3]](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/East_Africa#cite_note-3)At least during war time, each regiment could have multiple battalions. Men were recruited locally while officers, and at least some NCOs were from the British Army.

The _Army and Navy Gazette_ 15 February 1902 (page 2) stated

"We alluded recently to the creation of the King's African Rifles, under the Foreign Office, embodying the East and Central Africa and Uganda Forces, as an example of an organisation having many features to commend it, since it brings all units under a single and controlling responsible authority, and will cause the whole to be disciplined upon a simple system under settled rules and regulations.[[4]](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/East_Africa#cite_note-4)
Control of the King’s African Rifles appears to have passed to the Colonial Office in 1905.

From 1927 the administration of the King’s African Rifles, together with that of the Royal West Africa Frontier Force (previously The Niger and West Africa Frontier Force, known from 1900-1918 as the West Africa Frontier Force) was brought together in a new Military Branch within the Colonial Office. In September 1931 the appointments of inspector generals for the KAR and RWAFF were combined into one post; the Inspector General of African Colonial Forces.

The **East African Mounted Rifles** (EAMR) was a Volunteer regiment of settlers formed in Nairobi, Kenya, on 5 August 1914. Most of the members of the EAMR were expert riders, crack shots and they had the immense advantage of knowing the country, the conditions and the lingua franca of the country, Swahili. Within a few months many were transferred to other units to satisfy the demand for men who knew the country.[[5]](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/East_Africa#cite_note-5) Due to transfers, the regiment had faded away by May 1917.[[6]](https://wiki.fibis.org/w/East_Africa#cite_note-6)

The **Rhodesia Regiment** was in existence for various periods from 1899, including the Boer War and the First World War. Initially, many of the soldiers came from the Southern Rhodesia Volunteers. During the Second World War, the Battalions were only engaged in Home Service. Refer External links, below.

II of Ethiopia |

Between 1900 and 1920, the [British](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), assisted by the Ethiopians and [Italians](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy"), fought a series of **campaigns in Nugaal**—sometimes called the **Anglo-Dervish War**—against the Dervish kingdom of Diiriye Guure, and his successor nicknamed the "Mad Mullah" by the British, although he "was neither mad nor a mullah".[[1]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-1) During the [First World War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/First_World_War "First World War") (1914–1918), Sultan Diiriye Guure received aid from the [Ottomans](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"), [Germans](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") and, for a time, from the Emperor Iyasu V of Ethiopia. The conflict ended when the British [bombed the Dervish capital of Taleh](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign_(1920) "Somaliland campaign (1920)") in January–February 1920.

In the colonial period, the modern-day territory of Khatumo in the Horn of Africa were collectively referred to as "Nugaal".

### British Somaliland[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FNugaal_campaign%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

Main article: British Somaliland

Although nominally part of the [Ottoman Empire](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"), Yemen and the _sahil_ (including Zeila) came progressively under the control of [Muhammad Ali](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_of_Egypt "Muhammad Ali of Egypt"), ruler of [Egypt](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Egypt "Egypt"), between 1821 to 1841.[[2]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Clifford289-2) After the Egyptians withdrew from the Yemeni seaboard in 1841, _Haj_ Ali Shermerki, a successful and ambitious Somali merchant, purchased from them executive rights over Zeila. Shermerki's governorship had an instant effect on the city, as he manoeuvred to monopolize as much of the regional trade as possible, with his sights set as far as Harar and the Ogaden.[[3]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Abir-3) Shermerki was later succeeded as Governor of Zeila by Abu Bakr Pasha, a local Afar statesman.[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Lewismhs-4)

In 1874–75, the Egyptians obtained a _firman_ from the Ottomans by which they secured claims over the city. At the same time, the Egyptians received British recognition of their nominal jurisdiction as far east as Cape Guardafui.[[2]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Clifford289-2) In actuality, however, Egypt had little authority over the interior and their period of rule on the coast was brief, lasting only a few years (1870–84).[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Lewismhs-4)

The British Somaliland [protectorate](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") was subsequently established in the late 1880s, after the ruling Somali authorities signed a series of protection treaties granting the British access to their territories on the northwestern coast. Among the Somali signatories were the Gadabuursi (1884), Habar Awal (1884 and 1886),[[5]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Lewisapd-5) and Warsangali.[[6]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Laitinsam-6)

When the Egyptian garrison in Harar was eventually evacuated in 1885, Zeila became caught up in the competition between the Tadjoura-based French and the British for control of the strategic Gulf of Aden littoral. By the end of 1885, the two powers were on the brink of armed confrontation, but opted instead to turn negotiations.[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Lewismhs-4) They later signed a convention on 1 February 1888 defining the border between French Somaliland and British Somaliland.[[7]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Ravenstein-7)

### Italian Somaliland[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FNugaal_campaign%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

Main article: Italian Somaliland

[![Image 17: One of the forts of the in ](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Garesadihafun.jpg/250px-Garesadihafun.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a7/Garesadihafun.jpg)

One of the forts of the Majeerteen Sultanate in Hafun

The Majeerteen Sultanate within the northeastern part of the Somali territories was established in the mid-18th century and rose to prominence the following century, under the reign of the resourceful _Boqor_ (King) Osman Mahamuud.[[8]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Metz-8)

In late December 1888, Yusuf Ali Kenadid, the founder and first ruler of the Sultanate of Hobyo, requested Italian protection, and a treaty to that effect was signed in February 1889, making Hobyo an Italian protectorate. In April, Yusuf's uncle and rival, _Boqor_ Osman, requested a protectorate from the Italians and was granted it.[[9]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess416-9) Both Boqor Osman and Sultan Kenadid had entered into the protectorate treaties to advance their own expansionist goals, with Sultan Kenadid looking to use Italy's support in his ongoing power struggle with Boqor Osman over the Majeerteen Sultanate, as well as in a separate conflict with the Sultan of Zanzibar over an area to the north of Warsheikh. In signing the agreements, the rulers also hoped to exploit the rival objectives of the European imperial powers so as to more effectively assure the continued independence of their territories. The terms of each treaty specified that Italy was to steer clear of any interference in the sultanates' respective administrations.[[10]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Issa-Salwe-10)

In return for Italian arms and an annual subsidy, the Sultans conceded to a minimum of oversight and economic concessions.[[9]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess416-9) The Italians also agreed to dispatch a few ambassadors to promote both the sultanates' and their own interests.[[10]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Issa-Salwe-10) The new protectorates were thereafter managed by Vincenzo Filonardi through a chartered company.[[9]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess416-9) An Anglo-Italian border protocol was later signed on 5 May 1894, followed by an agreement in 1906 between Cavalier Pestalozza and General Swaine acknowledging that Baran fell under the Majeerteen Sultanate's administration.[[10]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Issa-Salwe-10)

### 1900–01[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FNugaal_campaign%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The first offensive campaign was led by Hassan against Ethiopian encampment at Jijiga in March 1900. The Ethiopian general Gerazmatch Bante reportedly repulsed the attack and inflicted great losses on the Dervishes, although the British vice-consul at Harar claimed the Ethiopians out of fear armed children with rifles to inflate the size of their forces. Hassan seized control of the Ogaden but did not attack Harar. Instead, he raided the non-Dervish Qadariyyah clans for their camels and arms.[[11]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess420-11) In 1901, the British joined with the Ethiopians and attacked the Dervishes with a force 17,000 strong. Hassan was driven across the border into the Majeerteen Sultanate, which had been incorporated into the Italian protectorate.[[11]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess420-11) The Ethiopians failed to get a hold on the western Ogaden and the British were eventually forced to retreat, having accomplished none of their goals. In this campaign, "borders were ignored by both British and Somali."[[11]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess420-11)

### February–June 1903[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FNugaal_campaign%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

[![Image 18: Cavalry and fort belonging to the ](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Hobyo_Sultanate_Cavalry_And_Fort.jpg/250px-Hobyo_Sultanate_Cavalry_And_Fort.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Hobyo_Sultanate_Cavalry_And_Fort.jpg)

Cavalry and fort belonging to the Sultanate of Hobyo

The British became convinced of their need of Italian assistance, but memories of the disastrous [Battle of Adowa](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Adowa "Battle of Adowa") inhibited any Italian fervour for action in the Horn of Africa. In 1903, the Italian Foreign Ministry permitted the British to land forces at Hobyo (Obbia). An Italian naval commander off Hobyo feared "that the expedition will end in a fiasco; the Mad Mullah will become a myth for the British, who will never come across him, and a serious worry for ... our sphere of influence."[[12]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-12)

The relationship between Hobyo and Italy soured when Sultan Kenadid refused the Italians' proposal to allow British troops to disembark in his Sultanate so that they might then pursue their battle against the forces of Diiriye Guure's Dervish kingdom.[[10]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Issa-Salwe-10) Viewed as too much of a threat by the Italians, Kenadid was exiled first to the British-controlled Aden Protectorate, and then to Italian Eritrea, as was his son Ali Yusuf, the heir apparent to his throne.[[13]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Sheik-Abdi-13) In May, the British Foreign Office realised the error, and had Kenadid's son appointed regent, just in time to forestall an attack in Mudug by the Sultan's army.[[14]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess421-14)

The expedition ended in failure soon after. Garad Diiriye Guure defeated a British detachment near Gumburru and then another near Daratoleh. With 1,200–1,500 rifles, 4,000 ponies and some spearmen, he occupied the Nugal Valley from Halin in the British protectorate to Ilig (or Illig) on the Italian-held coast. The main British force near Galad (Galadi) under General [William Manning](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/William_Manning_(colonial_governor) "William Manning (colonial governor)") retreated north along the line Bohotleh–Burao–Sheekh. This "old-established line" had already been breached by Sultan Deria Gure when he invaded the Nugal.[[15]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-15) By the end of June, the withdrawal was complete.

### January–May 1904[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FNugaal_campaign%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D7&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

After the failure of General Manning's offensive, General [Charles Egerton](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Charles_Egerton_(Indian_Army_officer) "Charles Egerton (Indian Army officer)") was entrusted with a response. Following extensive preparations, he united his field force at Bacaadweeyn (Badwein) on 9 January 1904 and defeated the kingdom of Diiriye Guure at Jibdalli the next day. The British and their allies from Hobyo harassed Diiriye Guure along his retreat, and he lost many of his camels and livestock throughout February.[[16]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-16) In early March, the second phase of operations began. The Ethiopians advanced as far as Gerlogubi, but turned back in early April. The [Italian Navy](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Regia_Marina "Regia Marina") bombarded Ilig in the winter to no effect. On 16 April, some ships of the [East Indies Station](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/East_Indies_Station "East Indies Station") under Rear Admiral [George Atkinson-Willes](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/George_Atkinson-Willes "George Atkinson-Willes") left Berbera to bombard Ilig in cooperation with an advance overland.[[17]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-17) The capture of Ilig was effected on 21 April, the British losing 3 men killed and 11 wounded, and the Dervishes 58 killed and 14 wounded. The naval detachment which had fought the battle remained ashore for four days, assisted by an Italian naval detachment that arrived on 22 April. Control of Ilig was finally relinquished to Ali Yusuf of Hobyo.[[18]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-18) Having defeated his forces in the field and forced his retreat, the British "offered the Mullah safe conduct into permanent exile at Mecca"; Hassan, the emir of king Diiriye Guure, did not reply.[[14]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Hess421-14)

### 1920[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FNugaal_campaign%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D8&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

[![Image 19: English camel troopers in 1913, between Berbera and in British Somaliland.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Engelse_kameelruiters_-_English_camel_troopers.jpg/250px-Engelse_kameelruiters_-_English_camel_troopers.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Engelse_kameelruiters_-_English_camel_troopers.jpg)

English camel troopers in 1913, between Berbera and Odweyne in British Somaliland.

Following the end of [World War I](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), British troops once again turned their attention to the disturbances in British Somaliland. The Dervishes had previously defeated British forces at the [Battle of Dul Madoba](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Dul_Madoba "Dul Madoba") in 1913. Four subsequent British expeditions against Hassan and his soldiers had also failed.[[19]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Baker-19)

In 1920, British forces launched a [final campaign](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign_(1920) "Somaliland campaign (1920)") against Hassan's Dervishes. Although the majority of the combat took place in January of the year, British troops had begun preparations for the assault as early as November 1919. The British forces were led by the [Royal Air Force](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") and the ground component included the [Somaliland Camel Corps](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_Camel_Corps "Somaliland Camel Corps"). After three weeks of battle, the Dervishes were finally defeated, bringing an effective end to their 20 year resistance.[[19]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Somaliland_campaign#cite_note-Baker-19)

The King's African Rifles
-------------------------

[![Image 2: 28 September 1941. Personnel from the King's African Rifles (KAR) collect weapons surrendered by Italian forces at Pass, , following the end of the . (Photographer: Lt H. J. Clements](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/KAR_soldiers_collecting_arms_at_Wolchefit_Pass.jpg/330px-KAR_soldiers_collecting_arms_at_Wolchefit_Pass.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/KAR_soldiers_collecting_arms_at_Wolchefit_Pass.jpg)

28 September 1941. Personnel from the King's African Rifles (KAR) collect weapons surrendered by Italian forces at Wolchefit Pass, [Ethiopia](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"), following the end of the [East African Campaign](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/East_African_Campaign_(World_War_II) "East African Campaign (World War II)"). (Photographer: Lt H.J.Clements.)

The **King's African Rifles** (KAR) was a multi-[battalion](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battalion "Battalion")British colonial regiment raised from the various British possessions in East Africa from 1902 until independence in the 1960s. It performed both military and internal security functions within the East African colonies as well as external service as recorded hereafter. Rank and file were Africans called askaris, while most officers were seconded from [British Army](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/British_Army "British Army") regiments. When raised there were some Sudanese officers in the Uganda-raised battalions and towards the end of British colonial rule African officers were commissioned in the various battalions.

*   [1 Uniforms](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#Uniforms)
*   [2 Formation](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#Formation)
*   [3 Operational history](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#Operational_history)
    *   [3.1 First World War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#First_World_War)
    *   [3.2 Inter-war period](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#Inter-war_period)
    *   [3.3 Second World War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#Second_World_War)
    *   [3.4 After the Second World War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#After_the_Second_World_War)

Uniforms[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FThe_King%2527s_African_Rifles%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[![Image 3: Four soldiers of the King's African Rifles at the coronation of in 1902.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Four_soldiers_of_King_Edward_VII%27s_African_Rifles_by_Sir_%28John%29_Benjamin_Stone.jpg/330px-Four_soldiers_of_King_Edward_VII%27s_African_Rifles_by_Sir_%28John%29_Benjamin_Stone.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f8/Four_soldiers_of_King_Edward_VII%27s_African_Rifles_by_Sir_%28John%29_Benjamin_Stone.jpg)

Four soldiers of the King's African Rifles at the coronation of [King Edward VII](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Edward_VII_of_the_United_Kingdom "Edward VII of the United Kingdom") in 1902.

Until independence, the parade uniform of the KAR comprised [khaki](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Khaki "Khaki") drill with tall fezes and cummerbunds. Both items were normally red, although there were some battalion distinctions with Nyasaland units, for example, wearing black fezes.

Prior to 1914, the regiment's field service uniforms reflected its constabulary role and consisted of a dark blue Jersey and puttees, khaki shorts and a khaki fez cover with integral foldable cloth peak and neck flap. African askaris wore sandals or were barefoot, on the rationale that the heavy military boots of the period were unsuitable for recruits who had not previously worn footwear.[[1]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#cite_note-1) Fezzes bore an Arabic or Roman number with the wartime raised battalions wearing theirs on geometric-shaped patches of cloth. During the Great War, all the dark blue items were replaced with khaki equivalents, and a short [pillbox hat](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Pillbox_hat "Pillbox hat") with a khaki cover was worn on campaign. After the war, the khaki shirt was replaced by a collarless blue-grey angora shirt called a "greyback".

Formation[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FThe_King%2527s_African_Rifles%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Six [battalions](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battalion "Battalion") were formed in 1902 by the amalgamation of the Central Africa Regiment, East Africa Rifles and Uganda Rifles, with one or two battalions located in each of Nyasaland, Kenya, [Uganda](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") and British Somaliland:

*   1st (Nyasaland) Battalion [1902–1964]
*   2nd (Nyasaland) Battalion [1902–1963]

Both the 1st and 2nd Battalions were also known as the 1st and 2nd Central African Battalions

*   3rd (Kenya) Battalion [1902–1963]
*   4th (Uganda) Battalion [1902–1962]
*   5th (Uganda) Battalion [1902–1904]—the Senior Battalion as it was the first to be raised.
*   6th (British Somaliland) Battalion [1902–1910]

The 5th and 6th battalions were subsequently disbanded by 1910 as a cost-saving measure by the Colonial Office and out of white settler concern over the existence of a large trained and indigenous armed force.

Operational history[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FThe_King%2527s_African_Rifles%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The King's African Rifles took part in the campaigns against [Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Mohammed_Abdullah_Hassan "Mohammed Abdullah Hassan") in Somalia during the early 1900s. Hassan was known to the British as the "Mad Mullah", though he was neither mad nor a mullah. The KAR were part of the British air and ground force that defeated Hassan in 1920.

[![Image 4: 3rd Bn KAR in 1902](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/The_National_Archives_UK_-_CO_1069-144-3.jpg/250px-The_National_Archives_UK_-_CO_1069-144-3.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/df/The_National_Archives_UK_-_CO_1069-144-3.jpg)

3rd Bn KAR in 1902

### First World War[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FThe_King%2527s_African_Rifles%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The KAR began the [First World War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") with 21 small companies in three battalions (each with up to eight companies following the British pre-1913 half-company [establishment](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Table_of_Organization_and_Equipment "Table of Organization and Equipment")): the 1st Nyasaland (half of the battalion was located in northeast Nyasaland), 3rd East Africa (with one company on Zanzibar) and the 4th Uganda, both of the latter included a 4th platoon of Sudanese with the 4th platoons of 4th battalion being led by Sudanese officers. Additionally the companies were scattered all over British East Africa.

Full strength of the KAR in 1914 was 70 British officers, three British NCOs, and 2,325 Africans. There were no organic heavy weapons (each company had only one machine gun), including artillery or organised reserves and the companies were in reality large platoons of 70 to 80 men.

In 1915 the KAR was expanded by having the three battalions reorganised into standard four-company battalions, which were then brought up to full strength at 1,045 men each. It was not until early 1916 that the 2nd Nyasaland and 5th Kenya battalions [1916–1963] were re-raised, this had more to do with white settler and South African sensitivities about arming and training large numbers of black African troops. Later in 1916 the 2nd, 3rd and 4th battalions were expanded into two battalions each through recruiting in their home areas. It was not until General Hoskin (formerly the [Inspector General](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Inspector_General "Inspector General") of the KAR) was appointed to command British East African forces in 1917 that genuine expansion began. The 1st Battalion was doubled and the 6th (Tanganyika Territory) Battalion was raised from [askaris](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Askari "Askari") of the former [German East Africa](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/German_East_Africa "German East Africa") and then it too was doubled. The 7th was formed from the Zanzibar Armed Constabulary and the Mafia Constabulary. Later in 1917 many other duplicate battalions were created as the first four battalions (now called regiments in the British tradition) each raised a 3rd battalion and a 4th or Training Battalion. The 4th Regiment raised an additional two battalions, the 5th and 6th through recruiting in Uganda. The KAR Mounted Infantry Unit (on camels), originally part of the 3rd regiment and the KAR Signals Company were also raised.

Thus in late 1918 the KAR consisted of 22 battalions as follows:

*   Western Force: 1st KAR Regiment with 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Battalions; plus 1st and 2nd Battalions 4th KAR Regt
*   Eastern Force: 2nd KAR Regiment with 1st, 2nd and 3rd Battalions; plus 3rd and 4th Battalions 4th KAR Regt
*   German East Africa Garrison: 3rd Battalion of the 3rd KAR, 5th battalion of the 4th KAR, 2nd battalion of the 6th KAR, 1st Battalion of the 7th KAR.
*   British East Africa Garrison: 1st Battalion of the 5th KAR, 1st Battalion of the 6th KAR
*   KAR Training Force: 4th Battalion 1st KAR, 4th Battalion 2nd KAR, 4th Battalion 3rd KAR, 6th Battalion 4th KAR

Part of the KAR's expansion involved bringing up unit strengths to the same size as British and [Indian Army](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Indian_Army "Indian Army")[Imperial Service units](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Imperial_Service_Troops "Imperial Service Troops"), while also increasing the numbers of white officers and NCOs. The increase in cadres was difficult due to the shortage of Swahili speaking whites, as many white settlers had already formed segregated units such as the [East African Mounted Rifles](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/East_African_Mounted_Rifles "East African Mounted Rifles"), the East African Regiment, the Uganda Volunteer Rifles and the [Zanzibar Volunteer Defence Force](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Zanzibar_Volunteer_Defence_Force "Zanzibar Volunteer Defence Force").

The regiment fought in the [East African Campaign](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/East_African_Campaign_(World_War_I) "East African Campaign (World War I)") against the German commander [Paul Erich von Lettow-Vorbeck](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Paul_Erich_von_Lettow-Vorbeck "Paul Erich von Lettow-Vorbeck") and his forces in German East Africa. Transport and support into the interior was provided by over 400,000 porters of the [Carrier Corps](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Carrier_Corps "Carrier Corps").

By the end of the Great War the KAR comprised 1,193 British officers, 1,497 British NCOs and 30,658 Africans (33,348 total) in 22 battalions, including two made up of former German askaris, as noted above. In _Armies in East Africa 1914–18_, Peter Abbot notes that the KAR units recruited from former prisoners of war were used as garrison troops by the British, to avoid any conflict of loyalties. However, one of these battalions was involved in the pursuit of a force under Hauptman Wintgens from February to October 1917.

KAR casualties in the First World War were 5,117 killed and wounded with another 3,039 dying from diseases.

### Inter-war period[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FThe_King%2527s_African_Rifles%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

During the [interwar period](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Interwar_period "Interwar period"), the KAR was slowly demobilised to a peace time establishment of 6 battalions, at which strength the Regiment remained until the Second World War. In 1938, the Regiment was composed of two brigade-strength units organised as a "Northern Brigade" and a "Southern Brigade." The combined strength of both units amounted to 94 officers, 60 non-commissioned officers, and 2,821 African other ranks. After the outbreak of war, these units provided the trained nucleus for the rapid expansion of the KAR. By March 1940, the strength of the KAR had reached 883 officers, 1,374 non-commissioned officers, and 20,026 African other ranks.[[2]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#cite_note-Mollo133-2)

### Second World War[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FThe_King%2527s_African_Rifles%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

[![Image 5: Training in Kenya c](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/KAR_Kenya.jpg/330px-KAR_Kenya.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/98/KAR_Kenya.jpg)

Training in Kenya c. 1944

The KAR fought in several campaigns during the [War of 1939–1945](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). It fought against the Italians in Italian East Africa during the [East African Campaign](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/East_African_Campaign_(World_War_II) "East African Campaign (World War II)"), against the Vichy French in Madagascar during the [Battle of Madagascar](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Madagascar "Battle of Madagascar"), and against the Japanese in Burma during the [Burma Campaign](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Burma_Campaign "Burma Campaign").

Initially the KAR was deployed as the 1st East African Infantry Brigade and the 2nd East African Infantry Brigade. The first brigade was responsible for coastal defence and the second for the defence of the interior. (See [1st SA Infantry Division)](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/1st_Infantry_Division_(South_Africa) "1st Infantry Division (South Africa)") By the end of July 1940, two additional East African brigades were formed, the 3rd East African Infantry Brigade and the 6th East African Infantry Brigade. Initially a Coastal Division and a Northern Frontier District Division were planned, but, instead, the [11th African Division](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/1st_(African)_Division_(United_Kingdom) "1st (African) Division (United Kingdom)") and the [12th African Division](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/2nd_(African)_Division_(United_Kingdom) "2nd (African) Division (United Kingdom)") were formed.

The two divisions included East African, Ghanaian, Nigerian, and South African troops. The Ghanaian and Nigerian troops came from the [Royal West African Frontier Force](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Royal_West_African_Frontier_Force "Royal West African Frontier Force"). Under the terms of a war contingency plan, a brigade each was provided from the Gold Coast (now Ghana) and from Nigeria for service in Kenya. A Nigerian brigade, together with two East African brigades (the KAR brigades) and some South Africans, formed the 11th African Division. The 12th African Division was similarly formed, but with the Ghanaian brigade instead of the Nigerian brigade.

In 1941, during the East African Campaign, Sergeant [Nigel Gray Leakey](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Nigel_Gray_Leakey "Nigel Gray Leakey") of the 1/6th Battalion was awarded the regiment's first and only [Victoria Cross](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Victoria_Cross "Victoria Cross") (VC).

[![Image 6: Troops of 11th East African Division on the road to Kalewa, Burma, during the Chindwin River crossing.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/African_Troops_in_Burma_during_the_Second_World_War_SE1884.jpg/250px-African_Troops_in_Burma_during_the_Second_World_War_SE1884.jpg)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f1/African_Troops_in_Burma_during_the_Second_World_War_SE1884.jpg)

Troops of 11th East African Division on the road to Kalewa, Burma, during the Chindwin River crossing.

The [11th African Division](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/1st_(African)_Division_(United_Kingdom) "1st (African) Division (United Kingdom)") was disbanded in November 1941 and the [12th African Division](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/2nd_(African)_Division_(United_Kingdom) "2nd (African) Division (United Kingdom)") was disbanded in April 1943. In 1943, the [11th (East Africa) Division](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/11th_(East_Africa)_Division "11th (East Africa) Division") was formed and it fought in Burma. In addition, two independent infantry brigades were sent from East Africa to India for service in Burma. The 22 (East Africa) Infantry Brigade served in the Arakan under command of XV Indian Corps, while the 28th (East Africa) Infantry Brigade served under IV Corps, playing a crucial role in the crossing of the Irrawaddy River.

By the end of the war the regiment had raised forty-three battalions (including two in British Somaliland), nine independent garrison companies, an armoured car regiment, an artillery unit, as well as engineer, signal and transport sections.

### After the Second World War[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FThe_King%2527s_African_Rifles%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D7&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The regiment played a major role in operations against the insurgents during the [Mau Mau Uprising](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Mau_Mau_Uprising "Mau Mau Uprising") in Kenya. In 1952, the 7th (Kenya) Battalion was reformed. It was renumbered as the 11th (Kenya) Battalion in 1956. 2nd/3rd Battalion, a reserve unit, was raised during the military phase of the emergency in Kenya and was under consideration for disbandment by 1957.[[3]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#cite_note-3)

The 1st, 2nd and 3rd battalions saw service in the [Malayan Emergency](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Malayan_Emergency "Malayan Emergency"), where they were heavily involved in fighting Communist rebels, suffering 23 dead.

The regiment was retitled the East African Land Forces in 1957. The last [Colonel-in-Chief](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Colonel-in-Chief "Colonel-in-Chief") of the KAR was [HM Queen Elizabeth II](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II").

When the various territories from which the KAR was recruited became independent, the regiment began to break up:

*   1st Battalion—1st Battalion, [Malawi Rifles](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Malawi_Rifles "Malawi Rifles")
*   2nd Battalion—2nd Battalion, Northern Rhodesia Regiment (subsequently Zambia Regiment)
*   3rd Battalion—3rd Battalion, Kenya Rifles[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#cite_note-KY10-4)
*   4th Battalion—1st Battalion, Uganda Rifles (later formed basis of the [military of Uganda](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Uganda_People%27s_Defence_Force "Uganda People's Defence Force"))
*   5th Battalion—5th Battalion, Kenya Rifles[[4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/The_King's_African_Rifles#cite_note-KY10-4)
*   6th Battalion—1st Battalion, [Tanganyika Rifles](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Tanganyika_Rifles "Tanganyika Rifles")
*   11th Battalion—11th Battalion, Kenya Rifles
*   26th Battalion—2nd Battalion, Tanganyika Rifles

The extent to which KAR traditions influence the modern national armies of the former East African colonies varies from country to country. In Tanzania, a mutiny in 1964 led to a conscious decision to move away from the British military model. In Kenya, on the other hand, the title of Kenya Rifles survives and the various campaigns in which the KAR distinguished itself in both World Wars are still commemorated.

The colours had many of the regiment's [battle honours](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_honour "Battle honour") emblazoned on it. The old colours were replaced in the 1950s.

1.content:
![Image 1: Single white dot on black background](http://samilitaryhistory.org/mhslogo1.gif) The South African

 Military History Society

* * *

Die Suid-Afrikaanse Krygshistoriese Vereniging
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

* * *

The Search for the May Jackson - Screw Gun Extraordinaire
---------------------------------------------------------

It was last seen in the Police Military Museum in the Old Boma in Lusaka in 1962-64 prior to Zambian Independence. The Boma has been demolished and the location of the contents are at present unknown.

**MAY JACKSON, SCREW GUN STAR**
A new 2.5 Inch Rifled Muzzle Loading Seven Pounder Mountain Gun was brought into service with the Royal Artillery in 1880. The gun was designed by Col. C B Le Mesurier RA so that the muzzle and breech, together 5 ft 9 inches long, could be separated for transit (hence 'the screw gun'). Each battery mule carried a load of 200-226lbs. One beast carried the muzzle (198.323lbs), one the breech (200lbs), one the carriage, one the two wheels, and a fifth the axle, coupling block, trunnion guard, elevating gear (a wedge & screw) and two storage boxes. Others carried ammunition and tools. The weapon could be carried in the same way by camels. It replaced a short barrelled seven pounder. The new gun was made of steel and rifled with 8 grooves with progressive curves. The trunnion ring was wrought iron. The wheels could be fastened to a hook at the back of the carriage to prevent recoil (the 'spade' presumably, a common device before recoil springs came in). The projectiles were fired by a gun charge of 6 ounces of black powder. Shells actually weighed 7.6lbs and contained a quarter pound powder charge. Shrapnel rounds containing 100 large and 11 small bullets with a 220 grain charge also weighed 7.6lbs. Case shot weighed 6.7lbs and contained 159 bullets. Star shells were also supplied. Projectiles came in cases of eight. Muzzle velocity was 1436ft per second and maximum range 4000 yards or 3,400 yards for shrapnel with time fuse.('The British Army, Sampson Low, Arston & Co 1899 reprinted as Scarlet into Khaki by Greenhill Books 1988 p130-1; Weapons & Equipment of the Victorian Soldier, Donald Featherstone, Blandford Press 1978 pp101-4).

The Royal Artillery had adopted breech loading guns in the 1860 but reverted to muzzle loaders in the 1870s until 1885 when field and horse batteries were again equipped with breech loaders. It was not until 1903 that the 7 pdr RBL was replaced in the regular mountain batteries of the Royal Garrison Artillery and the Indian Mountain Artillery by a new 10 pounder breech loading gun.

May Jackson was therefore only just over ten years out of date when she was sent north although by 1914 the 10 pdr was itself in process of replacement by the 12.75 gun firing a 12.5lb shell up to 5,600 yards (Allied Artillery of World War I Ian V Hogg, the Crowood Press 1998 p31). Mountain batteries RGA in India consisted of British gunners and Indian drivers. 10 Mountain Battery RGA in Natal had locally enlisted coloured muleteers. Indian mountain batteries each consisted of 50 per cent Sikhs and 50 per cent Punjabi Mussulmen.

The 'screw gun' lacked the elevation to make it an ideal mountain gun and the punch for conventional warfare. Carried by porters across the roadless plains and forests of tropical Africa against tribesmen with no artillery or long range weapons of their own it could breach most mud walls and wooden stockades and break up concentrations of warriors. Kipling made the 'Screw Gun' famous as the weapon of the mountain gunners but it also saw much service with the West African Frontier Force, the King's African Rifles and their predecessor units.

Seven pounders (perhaps the pre-1880 pattern) came to Rhodesia with the Pioneer Column in 1890. and remained in the British South Africa Company's armoury seeing action in the Matabele War in 1893. Two of these together with a twelve and a half pounder were lost in the Jameson Raid (Elizabeth Longford 'Jameson's Raid' 2nd Edition Weidenfelt & Nicolson 1982 p46 Jameson had three guns)

In the Regiment, (Covos Day Books 2000) at page 38, Reginald Hamley states that two guns belonging to 10 Mountain Battery RA were captured by the Boers at Majuba in 1881, subsequently recaptured and brought to Rhodesia, probably with the Matabele and Relief Force. It is true that a section (2 guns) of 10 Mountain Battery was sent up during the Matabele Rebellion of 1896, but not as part of Herbert Plumer's MRF which was a specially raised unit of mounted riflemen with Maxim machine guns but no artillery of its own. Another two seven- pounders were embarked at Cape Town to join Alderson's Mounted Infantry Battalion from Aldershot which landed at Beira in time to play its part in the suppression of the Mashona Rebellion. These two guns were originally sent with one officer, two NCOs and only four gunners who were to train settlers in their use. However Alderson shanghaied another eight Royal Artillerymen from the Garth Castle, a troopship bound for Mauritius. From the same source Alderson obtained a company of Sappers and a half company of the York and Lancaster Regiment including Sergeant F A Hodson. Colin Harding, a settler, returning from a break in England also attached himself to Alderson's command.

It is also true that Colley's force in 1881 included two 7 pounders and two 9 pounder guns.which were in action at Ingogo (Schuinshoogte) where two ammunition limbers fell into Boer hands.but no guns were taken up Majuba and none of these four guns were captured by the Boers. The 7 pounders had been in store in Durban, so were presumably the pre 1880 pattern and they were manned by infantrymen of the 60th Rifles. (Majuba 1881 Ian Castle Osprey Campaign Series) 10 Mountain Battery was not in South Africa at the time.

Seven pounders came to British Central Africa (Nyasaland) with the Indian Contingent of the Central African Rifles and were used with great effect in the suppression of the 'Ngoni Rebellion' of 1898 in North-Eastern Rhodesia.

When General Sir Ian Hamilton, as Inspector-General of Overseas Forces, inspected the BSAP in 1912 he found 3x7pdr 3" RML (was this the pre-1880 short barreled gun?), 4x7pdr 2.5" RML and one 75mm Quick Firing gun (presumably the 12 and a half pounder. Quick firing meant having a modern recoil system, a recuperator, and firing fixed ammunition, ie with the gun charge in a brass cartridge case issued in one piece with the shell) all in the care of 15 members of the Depot Staff trained as gunners (report in CO417/418 National Archives, Kew). He would not have mentioned anything which was obviously of no more than ornamental value. Sillitoe in 'Cloak without Dagger' talks of May Jackson squatting muzzle up on a parade ground with a plaque describing former glories but then says it reached Broken Hill covered in grease which suggests it had come out of store as it would surely not have been heavily greased for a rail journey of about 48hrs. Would Sillitoe have visited the Depot at Salisbury since he passed out of recruit training in 1908? Colonel Edwards, the Chief Commandant of Rhodesian Forces, would have wanted the most serviceable 7pdr sent to the Front with, one would hope the best available crew. 1709 Hadath, 1710 Hennessy and 1711 Horton appear to have all joined the BSAP in August 1913. Hopkins (1684 May? '13) who may have known them quite well said (NRJ p32) all three were ex Royal Dragoons. Since about half of the BSAP recruits of the period seem to have been former members of the mounted branches of the Regular Army and the Royal Dragoons were one of the only two British cavalry regiments stationed in South Africa at the time the regiment may have been specially well represented among recruits joining the BSAP in the last couple of years before World War I. 1762 B J Thomas, later the last British RSM of the NRP and first of the Northern Rhodesia Regiment was definitely ex-Royal Dragoons, but why choose them as gunners rather than former Horse and Field artillerymen. The fourth member of the crew 1866 John Farrar can only have joined the BSAP in July or August 1914 so perhaps he was a former regular gunner. We should not forget the six British South Africa Native Police who acted as ammunition numbers. Was one of these 4267 Kavuli who was mentioned in despatches?

A single screw gun in India would have been served by sergeant, a corporal, a bombardier and up to 13 gunners (there were 82 gunners in a six gun battery and about 180 drivers (10 Mountain Battery in 1899 had an establishment of 147 gunners for six guns!) and if separated from the rest of its battery would now doubt have been commanded by one of the 5 officers of the battery (Scarlet into Khaki p52.) The BSAP sent a newly promoted corporal and 9 men to operate hundreds of miles from their base under officers from another corps, albeit one closely connected with their own..

Lieutenant Percy Sillitoe having been ordered from his civil police duties at Lusaka to assemble 600 porters at Broken Hill, meet Horton's train there and and lead the whole caravan to Abercorn, there reverted to infantry duty. Horton and his crew were unable to reach Kasakalawe in time to engage the lakeborn raiders there on 19 November 1914 and May Jackson does not appear to have fired a shot in anger for more than six months. Her fame came at Saisi on 28 June and during the subsequent siege from 25 July until 3 August, putting a German gun out of action with a direct hit on its muzzle. She presumably remained at Saisi until the garrison was withdrawn on 29 October Abercorn. When Brig-Gen Edward Northey arrived on his preliminary inspection of his front and forces in March 1916. May Jackson was in post with a company of NRP at Zombe nine miles away.

When 'A' (Special Reserve) Company BSAP left Livingstone for the Northern Front in August 1915 it took the BSAP's 12 and a half pounder, (which appears to have been the twin of that taken by the Boers in the Jameson Raid). This gun under the veteran No.75 Sub-Inspector Charles Henry Chalmers had been sent from Salisbury with BSAP reinforcements on 8 July 1915 when the South African rebel Maritz was believed likely to try to break through from South West Africa. The gun was detrained at Kashitu 50 miles north of Broken Hill presumably so as to be able to make use of the wagon road cut through to Kasama by the Northern Rhodesia Rifles Mobile Column at the end of 1914. They had followed in the tracks Quincy's traction engine which had finally bogged down seven days march north of Chansa. Chalmers went down with enteric in January 1916 but recovered and did not return to Salisbury until 17 Nov 1917. He appears as Battery Sergeant-Major in the 1909 photo of BSAP NCOs opposite page 32 of 'Right of the Line'.

When Lt Col R E Murray DCM BSAP organised his Column for the advance on the German border fort of Namema, May Jackson was to be left at Abercorn and only the 12 and a half pdr and two newly arrived modern German 75mm mountain guns captured in SWA and manned by 5th Battery South African Mounted Riflemen were to accompany his Reserve Force. However Captain Langham claims to have seen May Jackson in action against Namema. She may well have been brought up between 23 May and 2 June 1916. Langham mentions the 12 and a half pounder but not the SAMR guns.

In any event May Jackson and the other BSAP gun did not accompany the advance further into German East Africa and by November 1918 had been backloaded from Abercorn to Kasama. The attempt to render them useless was probably made on the orders of Hector Croad who was intent on leaving nothing in Kasama that would be of use to the enemy.

I must have been mistaken in saying that 600 rounds of ammunition accompanied May Jackson to the Front. I cannot now find anything to gainsay Sillitoe's mention of 200 rounds. I must have confused the number of rounds with the number of porters. We don't know how many rounds May Jackson fired during the campaign. We know the Germans fired 40 into Abercorn on 8 September 1914 and 80 into Fife on 6 December.1915 and 216 enemy shells were reported to have been fired into Saisi (NA CO417/576). May Jackson can not have had many left from her 200 and, perhaps, at some stage she was re-supplied.

Of her crew John Farrar was invalided back to Salisbury on 17 March 1916. The other three all became machine gunners, saw the campaign through and were all awarded th Meritorious Service Medal. Jack Horton finished the War as an Acting Company Sergeant-Major in the Rhodesia Native Regiment. Edwin Hedath was a corporal when commissioned as a Temporary Second Lieutenant and John Hennessey became a sergeant.

From Rob Burrett
